newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Albright sees NATO-Russia progress amid problems.
newsitem.headline: Albright sees NATO-Russia progress amid problems.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Friday the United States and Russia had made progress on a European security deal, but there had been no breakthrough after two days of intensive talks.
Albright, speaking after talks with President Boris Yeltsin and Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, described the Russian leader as engaged and "very much in charge".
She was the first senior Western official to visit Yeltsin inside the Kremlin this year and the meeting marked another step for the president in reasserting his control of foreign policy.

Albright, on her first foreign tour since taking office, said there had been "important progress" on plans for a document defining post-Cold War ties between Russia and the NATO western alliance. But much complex work remained to be done.
She said it was far from certain that a deal could be in place by the July NATO summit in Madrid which will decide which former Soviet-bloc states to bring in as new members.
Primakov, describing Albright as "an Iron Lady but a constructive lady", said Russia remained firmly opposed to expansion of the alliance.
"We are...also trying to do everything possible to minimise the complications that may arise if expansion goes ahead," he said.
Russia has already warned NATO that its plans to grant membership to some of Moscow's Cold War allies in central and eastern Europe could upset the European security balance.
Moscow says NATO should sign a legally binding document on ties with Russia if expansion goes ahead, ceding some say to the Kremlin on future development.
The U.S. rejects the idea of a legally binding paper, although it says NATO has no plans to station nuclear weapons on the territory of new member states.

As part of the diplomatic offensive to calm Russian fears, NATO officials on Thursday presented its arms reduction plan to a body in Vienna dealing with the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty.
Moscow wants the treaty revised and NATO intended the proposal to soften soothe Moscow's fears that the alliance could pile up weapons on its borders.

The proposal would also establish a "sensitive geographic region" in Russia's Baltic enclave of Kaliningrad, Ukraine, Slovakia, Belarus, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland, in which ground equipment could not be increased.

In Moscow, Albright declined to comment on what diplomats privately say is a wildcard in NATO negotiations -- Yeltsin's health -- but said he was alert. The president had heart bypass surgery last November and is still recovering from pneumonia.
Reporters were given brief access at the start of the Kremlin meeting. Yeltsin's face looked pale and waxen.

Albright's spokesman said she had given Yeltsin a letter from U.S. President Bill Clinton discussing the likely agenda for a summit the two leaders plan to hold in Helsinki next month and outlining what they want to achieve there.

U.S. officials said the Czech-born Albright spoke Russian at the start and end of the meeting, dispensing with interpreters from Russian to English at the end because she understood and because she and Yeltsin wanted to speed up the talks.
Appealing directly to the Russian people at a news conference after her meeting with Primakov, she said Russia was now on the same side as its one-time NATO foes.
"We are no longer in a situation of you versus us. We are all on the same side," she said. "The new NATO is not the NATO of the Cold War."

The NATO-Russia package is designed to assuage Russian concerns about alliance expansion. That includes a charter or document defining NATO-Russia ties in the future and promises of vastly enhanced Russia-alliance cooperation.
